Second, on leadership, you have emphasized proactive diplomacy and full use of the tools provided by the Charter. Could you identify one current global crisis where, as Secretary-General, you would pursue a different approach from the current being taken by the United Nations and what outcome you will seek to achieve? Third, on reform, you have expressed support for the UN aid reform agenda and for a more agile and effective United Nations. If difficult budgetary decisions become necessary, what guiding principle would determine what organization must protect at all costs, and how would you ensure that United Nations remains both effective and true to his mandate to protect the most vulnerable. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Angola on behalf of the group of Portuguese-speaking countries. Please, Your Excellency.

Thank you to Ambassador of Angola for the questions. Oceans, I believe, is already central in the work of the United Nations, and whatever we can do to strengthen that, as Secretary-General, I would certainly do that. Including the implementation of the BBNG agreement, where support by member states is requested from the Secretariat. I am aware that a lot of work is being done on IUU fishing, particularly by the Food and Agriculture Organization. Some of this work was being done with some of the big tech companies in terms of satellite imaging, for example, to— Thank you. See where IUU fishing is taking place. And so, of course, we will leverage the entire system, including the work being done as FAO, and as Secretary-General, I would certainly do that. Because oceans, it's very important, of course, for your group, for small island developing states as well, and many times capacity is an issue on IUU fishing. On delivery of the SDGs, as I mentioned before, the issue of financing, would be a top priority, working with the IFIs, and also utilizing the tools that you member states have already approved, like the MVI and the work that is being done on Beyond GDP. This will be important tools, I think, as we engage the IFIs, particularly looking at vulnerability for those states that right now find it very difficult to access concessional financing, because of the frameworks that exist right now. In terms of identifying one global crisis, I think that would be a little bit difficult for the Secretary-General to do, I think, right now, given that there are a number of global crises and you don't want to be accused of having a hierarchy of crisis and how you see them. But what I certainly would do once I'm elected Secretary-General is to have an assessment or look at what is before me in terms of the assessment where the Secretary-General intervention might yield speedy results. And so that's how I would approach that. On the UNHCR reform agenda and the difficult financial situation and where budget cuts would be necessary and how I would approach that, I would be guided, of course, by member states but would provide that information that they need in making those decisions for cuts. In particular, I would provide information to ensure that we do not roll back on the development gains that we have made. And so the UN 8A agenda, as I see it, is a continuous review, because once we are implementing, we should be able to know whether these measures that we are implementing are good or that they are rolling back on our development gains, and that information I would provide to member states so that they could make the decisions that would be appropriate.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Kenya on behalf of the UNAID Global Group.

Thank you, Madam President. I wish to raise the following question on behalf of the UNHCR global group, across regional group of member states that includes Barbados, Indonesia, Jordan, Mexico, New Zealand, Norway, Senegal, Singapore, and my own country, Kenya. Excellency, Ms. Caroline Rodriguez-Birkett, should you be selected as the next Secretary-General, What will you do to maintain and strengthen trust between the Secretariat and the Member States, the Executive Office of the Secretary-General and the rest of the system, and the global confidence in the UN? I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Kenya on behalf of the UNAID Global Group. Please, Secretary-General.

Thank you to Kenya, as I said in my vision statement, I would be accessible to all member states, but also I'll be proactive in meeting with member states, in particular the permanent representatives that are based here in New York. Any proposal that I would make, before I do so, I will be consulting with member states across the UN. And so that would be my approach in terms of strengthening the relationship between my office and member states, but also the wider Secretariat. Trust-building, I think, is an ongoing activity for all of us, and member states must have the confidence in the Secretariat, and the Secretariat, of course, must also always be available for two member states. In terms of global confidence in the United Nations, as I mentioned before, part of my vision— in part of my vision, I would like to improve the communication with our global publics. Many times I am told that there are difficulties in countries and parliaments receiving approval for funding for the United Nations. As a former foreign minister, I used to have to defend the contributions to organizations, international organizations, and I know how important the provision of information to not only the public but the Ministry of Finance was in that regard. And so I think it's important for us to say to our public, the work of the United Nations the good work that we are doing, the challenges we face, but also how we are going to address them. So that I would put a lot of focus on in communicating better, both at the country level but globally as well.

I thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Denmark on behalf of the Accountability, Coherence and Transparency Group, followed by the next civil society organization and Nepal.

Thank you, Madam President, and thank you to Ambassador Rodrigues-Becquet for presenting your candidacy here today. I wish you all the best of luck in your campaign. I would like to ask two questions on behalf of the Accountability, Coherence, and Transparency Group, also known as ACT. The ACT Group is a cross-regional group comprised of 27 small and mid-sized countries committed to a transparent and accountable UN and seeking to improve the working methods of the Security Council. So my questions are as follows. First, the selection and appointment process for the Secretary-General is fundamentally a joint process between the Security Council and the General Assembly, but it's not the only area where they have a complementary mandate. How do you see the role of the General Assembly in the maintenance of international peace and security? And the second question is, the General Assembly has underlined the importance for candidates to embody the highest standards of efficiency, competence, and integrity. The civil society organization One for Eight Billion has published a set of principles for integrity for Secretary-General campaigns and have asked all the candidates to commit to them. Are you willing to commit to these principles, and if not, why?

Thank you.

I thank the representative of Denmark on behalf of ACT. Ambassador Burkitt.

I thank the representative of Denmark for her question. In relation to the question on the role of the General Assembly in the maintenance of international peace and security, I think that role is very well prescribed already, and so I see the General Assembly being the wider community, and we must, I think, find ways to support members of the General Assembly as they implement that role. But as a Secretary-General, I would not be able to say to the General Assembly, this is exactly what you should do. This is a member state-driven responsibility, I would say. But I do know, and I cannot disregard it from my previous experience just recently, that there is a loud call for the General Assembly to play a greater role in the maintenance of international peace and security precisely because of the proliferation of global conflicts and the belief that more can be done by the Security Council and the General Assembly, and the importance for this to be communicated to our world. In terms of the principles that you ask whether I would abide with them, the answer is yes. Thank you.
Thank you. I now invite the Assembly to view a prerecorded video by Blue Africa Africa, Blue and Coastal Community.

Good day, ladies and gentlemen, all protocol observers. My name is Abiola Oyekon. I'm representing Blue Africa. I want to thank the organizer of this program for the opportunity to ask the UN Secretary General-designate question. My question centered on the UN Haiti Initiative and the legacy of the future summit, you know, which actually presents an opportunity to reshape the United Nations by raising the Secretary General's budget by 20% and also merge key agencies. Thank you. As the incoming Secretary-General, your leadership role is very critical in navigating the political complexity of this transformation. How will you ensure this drive for efficiency does not compromise the UN's ability to deliver on its core mandates? Thank you.
Ambassador Rijks.

Thank you, Ms. Fabiola, for your question. As I said in my opening statement, I believe that there is consensus that the UN can do things different and can do things better, and UN Haiti Initiative is a recognition of that. It is true that we are in a liquidity crisis, and we will have to make certain adjustments. And it's important that we, when we make those adjustments, that we do not compromise the efficiency. But I also believe that we could have a structural alignment that would preserve the functions of the various agencies, funds, and programs, and that we could be better able to deliver. As Secretary-General, as soon as I take office if elected. I would also look to see where we can have greater efficiencies and advise member states accordingly on that. But the truth is we do have a liquidity crisis and we have to work in some ways backwards to ensure that we do not reverse the gains that have been made. So that is why I said my vision is both realistic and pragmatic because these are the constraints that we face right now and we have to do better with less and we have to see how that will be done. But at the end of the day, I will work with member states on this.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the Republic of Korea, who is also speaking on behalf of Egypt, Myanmar, Norway, and Peru.

Thank you, Madam President. Thank you, Ambassador Lourdes Braguette, for joining us today. I have the honor to deliver these questions on behalf of Egypt, Myanmar, Norway, Peru, and my country, Republic of Korea, member states whose nationals have served as Secretary-General of the United Nations. The responsibilities entrusted to the Secretary-General under the Charter are profound. While the Charter designated the Secretary-General as the chief administrative office of the organization, it also assigned the office an independent political role in maintenance of international peace and security. As complex conflicts continue to unfold across the globe and calls for reform of the organization grow ever stronger, The United Nations require a Secretary-General who can successfully navigate both the political and managerial dimension of the role, equal parts diplomat and advocate, civil servant and CEO. As countries whose nationals have served as Secretary-General, our questions are, first, the office of the Secretary-General frequently require difficult judgment between principles and pragmatism, public advocate and quiet diplomacy, action and restraint. During your wide-ranging and long career in public service, have you ever faced such a situation where you have to make such difficult judgment? What lessons and principles from those experiences would guide you as Secretary-General? Second, looking at— you paid tribute to the former Secretary-Generals. Looking at the on-the-job experiences of previous Secretary-Generals, what lessons would you believe remain most relevant for the next Secretary-General? And in my national capacity, I would like to add one more question. At a time when the international community's attention is increasingly pulled in multiple directions, how can the UN ensure that longstanding challenges to peace and security, including those on Korean Peninsula, receive the sustained and consistent engagement they demand? I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea, also speaking on behalf Egypt, Myanmar, Norway, and Peru. Your Excellency.

I thank the representative of Korea for the question, and you did underscore that the Secretary-General is a chief administrative officer. I think the role has also evolved in terms of the expectations of member states to be much more than the chief administrative officer, chief diplomat, as the chief spokesperson, and certainly I will fulfill those expectations working with member states, I hope, bringing both my political experience and also my managerial experience to the task. I spoke about principled pragmatism in my opening statement. I do believe that pragmatism is extremely important, but I also believe that pragmatism without principles can sometimes border on what are not the right things to do. So principled pragmatism will certainly guide me. Throughout my career, I've never had to make a decision where something pragmatic might conflict with my principles. I have no illusions of this job, but I pray that I would never have to do that, and if I do, I would have to fall on the side of principle. In terms of what I've learned from past Secretary Generals, and I have been, of course, reading a bit from the work of past Secretary Generals, I know for sure they don't sleep a lot, but I also know that— In many of the cases, the conversations with member states and keeping closely in touch with permanent representatives helped to buoy the Secretary-General when making decisions, and that is something that I take from several of the past Secretary-Generals that I would apply should I become Secretary-General. I thank you.
I thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Nepal on behalf of the Least Developed Countries, followed by Singapore and Australia.

Thank you, Madam President. At the outset, the Least Developed Countries Group would like to thank you, Madam Carolina Druick-Breckert, for your clear, thoughtful, and substantive presentations. As you are aware, the least developed countries face the greatest structural vulnerabilities and challenges, and they are lagging the furthest behind in achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. On this, the LDC group would welcome Madam SG Candidate's views on the following questions. First, if elected as Secretary General, what concrete steps will you take to reestablish the United Nations LDCs as the central platform for addressing the global peace and security, development, and financing issues? And how will you ensure that LDCs meaningfully remain at the table to shape the decisions rather than remain on the margins? Second, what will be your strategic approach to mobilize and direct adequate, predictable, and consistent resources to LDCs and how will you reorient the UN deployment system so that supporting LDCs to achieve the SDGs and smooth, irreversible and sustainable graduation becomes a visible system-wide priority at country level? Third, in the face of the ongoing financial constraint, how will you ensure that the resources and dedicated support to LDCs, including to the LDC-dedicated UN mechanisms, are protected and strengthened rather than reduced, and what specific measures will you put in place? Fourth, as the UN faces unprecedented challenges from within and outside, which yourself highlighted during your presentations, what strategic approach will you undertake to reinvigorate the UN's development pillar to address problems like poverty eradication, inequality, social protections, and sustainable financing, and deliver transformative system-wide support for the LDCs, ensuring that the promise of the UN Charter translates into tangible, lasting progress to those furthest behind. I thank you.

Thank you.

Thank the distinguished representative of Nepal on behalf of the least developed countries. Your Excellency.

I thank the permanent representative of Nepal for his questions. We all say in the UN that we should leave no one behind, and I believe that the LDCs are some of the countries that if we do not advance on the development pillar are the most likely to be left behind. So this must be a priority for the entire United Nations, and certainly, as Secretary-General, it will be a priority for me. You indicated how— you asked how I would ensure that the LDCs are not on the sidelines of decision-making. I think that we have to work together to make sure that the LDC voices together are heard in all the different spaces and in all the negotiations that are taking place, specifically on the UN reform and Workstream 3, which is the structural alignment, because that is where the impact will be most in terms of UN delivery. I mentioned before the issue of financing and the work that I intend to do together with member states working with the IFIs to not only improve concessional financing, but also the general reform that would be needed to advance the SDGs. An important component of what I would like to focus on is also engagement with the private sector. There are lots of resources out there, but how we leverage the private sector, I think it will be very important, and so— Thank you. I will work to have very clear ideas on how we can do this to advance development. On the— ensuring the development pillar, it's all about that, that I just mentioned there, the deficit in the implementation of the SDGs. We are going to only be achieving 18% of the SDGs by 2030. The post-2030 framework we have to start thinking about that. Member States would have to start thinking about that shortly. But I also believe that the Pact for the Future, it's important in these discussions as we speak about implementation. After all, it was meant to turbocharge the implementation of the SDGs. Thank you, Madam President.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Singapore on behalf of the small states.

Thank you very much, Madam President, and a warm welcome to Ambassador Caroline Rodriguez-Birkett. On a personal note, let me say that I'm delighted to see that an experienced diplomat and an exemplary permanent representative has stepped forward as a candidate, and I wish her all the best. Madam President, I have the honor indeed to deliver this statement on behalf of the Small States Group.— a cross-regional grouping of small states comprising both developed and developing countries. More than 50 countries have aligned with this statement, and the list will be made available after the meeting. Ambassador Rodriguez-Birkett, as you well know, we are living in a volatile and dangerous period in international relations, characterized by geopolitical tension and conflict. For small states, an effective multilateral system founded on the principles of the UN Charter and international law is not an option, but an existential necessity. The next Secretary-General will play a critical role not only in defending the UN Charter, but also in reinvigorating and reshaping the role and relevance of the United Nations. We look to the Secretary-General to safeguard the interests of all Member States, especially the interests of the smallest, weakest, and most vulnerable members of the UN. We do not want a world of might is right, where international law and the sovereignty and territorial integrity of small states are violated with impunity. The members of the SSG stand ready to work with the next Secretary-General and all Member States to strengthen the role of the UN and to defend international law and multilateralism. In the interest of brevity, I will ask just two questions. First, what steps will you take to strengthen the role of the General Assembly, especially at a time when the Security Council has been unable to take decisive action And a related question: How will you support and strengthen the office of the President General— of President of the General Assembly? Second, we are at a critical moment when public perception of the United Nations seems to have become critical and even cynical in many countries. How do you plan to galvanize support for the work of the UN, especially among younger people around the world who represent the future in all our societies? Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Singapore on behalf of the Small States Group. Please, Your Excellency.

Thank you, Ambassador, for your questions on behalf of the Small States Group. I'm from a small state, and so I know the value of the United Nations. We find refuge in the Charter and international law, and by virtue of us being small states, we have to think big. So I am very much aware of the challenges facing small states as well. Some of the small states are, as you mentioned, smallest, weakest, most vulnerable, including, for example, small island developing states who face significant challenges when it comes to the impact of climate change. And so this certainly would be a priority as we go forward, how as Secretary-General I can work better with small states given the peculiarities that many of them face as well. In terms of the role of the General Assembly and how I can work to strengthen the office of the PGA, at the moment, as you know, the— Thank you. The Secretariat or the Secretary-General's role in this is providing the kind of secretarial services, Secretariat services to the PGA. Having been in these halls for the last 5 years, I've heard member states call for a more strengthened office of the PGA, and as Secretary-General, of course, whatever is decided by member states, I would work to ensure that those— that is implemented And even so, whoever is the PGA office in any particular year, as Secretary-General, I would work with the PGA to strengthen that office, making sure that it serves the political function that it was envisaged to serve to all of our people. Young people and how we galvanize young people. I know the benefits of when governments invest in young people. I became a minister at the age of 27, and during that time, it was a time when the ministers were much older than that, and I was the youngest in the cabinet, and the country was a little bit concerned. But a few years later, and even today, it is very difficult to hire someone that is less— that is older than 60. Yes. To serve in some of these things, so it created a sort of a wave. But for me as Secretary-General, I think it's important to communicate with our young people, to galvanize them for the support of the UN. They are the ones active on social media. They are the ones promoting the work of the UN, but I think we need to do more with them, especially where some of them don't even have access. Yes. As well to technology. But I'm all for the young, not that I disregard older people. Thank you.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Australia on behalf of Cairns, followed by Malawi and Palau.

Thank you, President, and Ambassador Carolyn. I don't think there's anybody in the room here or our community in New York who didn't let out a little cheer on your nomination, so a personal congratulations from all of us, of course. I speak for Canada, New Zealand, and of course my own country, Australia, but many of the questions have already preempted what I was going to ask, so I hope they forgive me if I modify a little bit. Three key points and then a question from me. Three key points is really, I think, what's so important about the new Secretary-General is that that person does whatever they can to rebuild institutional credibility, capability, and capacity. Secondly, I think we all look to the Secretary-General to strengthen the good offices role of the function, and we all recognize that requires political courage and effect, and we look to a future Secretary-General to bring that very much to the table. Finally, of course, in terms of points being made, we all recognize, or most recognize, the criticality of the three pillars underpinning the work of the United Nations, and the Secretary-General has a fundamental role in prosecuting that. By way of question, can I ask, all of us have talked a lot about UN 80 and the future of the enterprise. I'd be very interested in your reflections on what are the tangible things you think we can most functionally do out of UN 80, and do you have further ideas of your own as to what sort of reforms you would like to drive that go beyond perhaps what we've already considered. Thank you so much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Australia on behalf of CANES.

Thank you, Ambassador, for the question. You spoke about the institutional credibility and restoring the institutional credibility of the UN, and I know that that credibility has suffered over the years, mainly because, in my view, the UN is judged through the peace and security lens, but the UN is much wider than that and it's delivering in many, many areas— in development, in human rights. But we also face the situation— on the one hand, we want to restore the institutional credibility, so we want to make sure we deliver better, and on the other hand, we face the liquidity crisis. And the balancing of that, I think, would be important. And this is where UNETE, I think, is extremely important, and the work that you member states are doing. As I mentioned before, the good work on improving efficiencies in the Secretariat, we have to continue to do that. The mandate and how we treat with mandates, how member states would treat with mandates, that was a significant piece of work.— and perhaps can bring us to focus in a more laser way on the work of the UN in terms of mandates, but the structural reform aspects, structural alignment and programmatic alignment, I think that how member states proceed with that would be extremely, extremely important. And that is where I see the Secretary-General being central, not in terms of what the Secretary-General would like to see, because this is a member states-driven process, but providing member states with the information from an objective standpoint in terms of what this would mean for the UN's delivery. And, you know, that is going to take some time. I don't expect that that's going to finish by the time the new Secretary-General is in place, but as you know, the Secretary-General and the Secretariat is an implementer. Yes. But certainly got a role to play in providing that type of information. So in terms of tangible steps, that is what I see. I do not— I will confess that I don't have the entire panorama of what can be done in terms of the structural alignment, but this will be a top priority, and we have to safeguard the delivery of the UN to the most vulnerable countries, and in this regard, the RCEP system and how we strengthen that, notwithstanding the issues with liquidity, will be important. It would call for a lot of creativity, but I'm willing to delve into that, and this is where the team around me will be very, very important as well. Thank you.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Malawi on behalf of the African Group.

On behalf of the Africa Group, I thank you, Madam Caroline Roddickes, for presenting your priorities to us, and I would wish to hear from you on the following questions. One, Africa's exclusion from permanent membership of the Security Council reflects both a historical injustice and an ongoing structural inequity affecting decisions on issues central to the continent. What is your position on the Common African Position, and how would you use the convening authority of the office of the— of the office, if you are elected, to advance intergovernmental negotiations, commitment to Security Council reform, and African permanent membership with all prerogatives and privileges. Second, taken that the Security Council has primary responsibility for the maintenance of the international peace and security, Security Council Resolution 2719 created a framework of— for AU-led peace support operations authorized by the Security Council to access assessed contributions from the UN regular budget to ensure equitable, predictable, sustainable financing for AUPs and security offices. Yet implementation has stalled. How would you approach the third-year review, and what are the options you intend to propose to ensure an appropriate operationalization of this resolution that will serve the purpose of guaranteeing sustainable financial support to AU-led PSOs instead of shifting the burden to the African Union? What concrete actions would you take to advance reform of the international financial architecture, including improving African representation in the international financial institutions? How would you ensure that climate finance mechanisms, including the Loss and Damage Fund, are accessible to African countries and adequately resourced? Fifth, considering the organization's liquidity constraints, how would you safeguard development mandates and ensure sufficient funding for African-focused programs? Sixth, Africans remain underrepresented at senior levels. What targets would you set and what accountability mechanisms would you advise to ensure progress at P4, P5 level and above? I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Malawi on behalf of the African Group, Your Excellency.

Thank you. Let me speed answer, given the number. Let me start with the UN UN Security Reform. As you know, in my life yesterday, I was representing CARICOM as a coordinator in UNSC Reform, and I believe that what I have heard from many is that we have the consensus on UN Security Council reform, as indicated in the Pact for the Future. And it was a significant step that Africa was included in the pact singled out for— as a special case. And so I think those steps are very, very important. The common African position seemed to have widespread support. In terms of me as Secretary-General in this IGN process, the IGN process is member-state driven, but the Secretariat must always be ready to provide all the support that is needed in the context of the IGN. Thank you. Process, and hopefully we will be able to see some movement on Security Council reform as we move forward. On 2719, I believe that this resolution was a landmark resolution, both in terms of partnership and in terms of cost sharing as well between the UN and the African Union. In terms of what the Secretary-General can do, I think it's important for the Secretariat to be ready when the Security Council chooses a particular situation that they would like 2719 to be implemented or applied. And so, for now, is the Secretary-General ensuring the readiness of the organization to implement 2719. But I also believe that this is one of the experiments in terms of how we do peace operations. Peacekeeping. And it's important that whatever is done, that there is success. But for now, the Secretary-General will have to wait on the Security Council to identify that situation where 2719 could be applied. On the IFIs, I spoke about that and reform of the IFIs, but I was just recently listening to one of the presidents of Africa who spoke about— the continent having $4 trillion in insurance, and that heads of state in Africa are looking to see how that can be leveraged, and perhaps this is— there's a place for the UN support in doing that, and of course my office will be available to work there. On the Loss and Damage Fund, this is important that it be fully operationalized, and whatever the Secretary-General can do I would certainly work to do that. I know many countries still face a lot of challenges in applying for climate finance where they exist, and so that will be continued work as well. And on Africa senior levels, I've spoken about how I will treat with senior staff, ensuring geographical representation and merit.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Palau on behalf of the Alliance of Small Island States, followed by Uganda.

Madam President, thank you for convening this important dialogue, and I wish to thank Madam Rodriguez-Briket for your interaction with us today. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the 39 members of the Alliance of Small Island States, AOSIS. As a group of countries in special situations, the credibility of the United Nations lies in its ability to respond to the unique circumstances of SIDS, correct longstanding inequities, and deliver results for the most vulnerable. In this regard, allow me to, to pose the following questions: How will you, as Secretary-General, ensure that the United Nations system is more accessible, better coordinated, and tailored to the unique vulnerabilities of SIDS to better and more meaningfully support the full implementation of the Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS? Thank you. Second, how will you use your leadership to accelerate global ambition and action on climate change, particularly to keep 1.5 within reach while ensuring that SIDS receive scaled-up, predictable, and accessible finance for adaptation, mitigation, and loss and damage in line with international commitments? And finally, what specific measures will you take to improve on the underrepresentation of SIDS within the United Nations Secretariat, especially at senior leadership levels, And how will you strengthen pathways for SIDS nationals to shape decision-making across the United Nations? I thank you.
Please, Your Excellency, you have the floor.

I thank the representative of Palau for the question, and I know that member states did a lot of work in terms of the Antigua and Barbuda agenda for SIDS, and the implementation is now that what will be important. I also know that before the ABAS came into being, we had the Samoa Pathway and we did not get very far in the implementation of that, and so we have to dedicate all efforts in the implementation of the ABAS. So whatever the United Nations is involved in, it must be through the prism of the ABAS, the Agenda for SIDS. I've spoke about— spoken about this scaled-up finance and how I intend to use my office to advance the reform of the IFIs. I am aware that the Multidimensional Vulnerability Index is there. The issue is how we get that index to be used by the IFIs and the relevant banks, and so that requires a lot of advocacy, and as Secretary-General, of Of course, course, I will be advocating for that and using the other instruments, as I mentioned before, the work that is being done on Beyond GDP. I see them as complementary, but these are tools that I believe can help us to advance as we work with the international financial institutions. On the underrepresentation and unrepresent— underrepresented and unrepresented countries of SIDS in the UN, Coming from a CARICOM state, and we are in— consider Guyana is considered a SIDS as well. Just recently, we have been asking for information of the Secretariat on the unrepresented and underrepresented, and we know that there are several countries that are included in that group. One of the challenges that we learned from countries too is just the capacity to apply for the positions that are available within the UN, and sometimes our— the publics in the SIDS countries are not aware of what is available. So I think it would be important for the Secretary-General to ensure that countries, not only SIDS but other countries with capacity constraints to apply, are given the resources to do that in terms of the information that we that we have that could be helpful so that we have a pipeline. And so when we have the hiring, we will be able to have SIDS countries included there as well. In terms of the coordination of the UN system, I know that in the ABAS discussions, that there— the discussions focus on what's the best way for the UN to deliver. There are several offices that are working on SIDS. But certainly I know that SIDS in their meetings will be able to come to a position working with the Secretariat so that we have the best mechanism to deliver. Thank you.

Thank you. We have 11:38 and we have exhausted the allotted time for the first segment. While there is still interest from Member States to speak on the first segment, in the interest of time, I invite delegations to proceed to the second segment to allow sufficient time to hear the candidates' response to the question related to the three pillars of the United Nations: peace and security, development, and human rights, which has been mentioned already before by some delegations. As before, civil society questions will be interspersed with questions from member states. Priority will be given to those who have not spoken in the first segment. Madam President, I speak on behalf of the 121 member states of the Non-Aligned Movement. So consensus, majority, they both have their purpose and I think it helps to also show the state of multilateralism, if I may say that.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic.

Thank you very much, Madam President, and thank you very much to Ambassador Rodrigues Beckett for discussing very important issues to the members today. As you know, the peacekeeping operations, traditionally speaking, are going through an adaptation crisis given ever more fragmented transnational multidimensional crises. As part of the —current revision—review of peacekeeping operations, what strategic criteria do you think would be essential to guide the transition towards hybrid or non-traditional modalities, including operations authorized but not led by the United Nations? How would you ensure complementarity between those models and the multilateral collective security system, ensuring doctrinal coherence, clear mandates, and accountability when it comes to international humanitarian law? Thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Dominican Republic. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you for the questions. On peacekeeping or how we do peace operations, I know that there's a report with several models that are being proposed and that this would be something that member states would have to consider. The idea is that we are all aware that the nature of conflicts has changed and that we need different types of models for different situations. The challenge, of course, is to make sure the high standards of the UN in any of those models. Like I mentioned before, I see Resolution 2719 and that partnership for AU-led operations, and I also see the GSF in Haiti as two experiments in this regard, and how successful they are I think would be important for member states' consideration as we go forward in how we do peace. But whatever we do, and this— as Secretary-General, I think this is important, and I've included this in my vision statement— is that whether we're doing a traditional peacekeeping operation, a certain type of peace enforcement operation. It must be a means to an end, a means to a political solution, giving the space for a political solution to move forward. So they must be accompanied— peace operations must be accompanied by a pathway for political solutions. And as Secretary-General, it would be important for me to provide that information to the Security Council, and what are some of the possible political solutions that could be pursued. I thank you.
I thank you. I now give the floor to our last civil society organization in this interactive dialogue, the Women's Refugee Commission. Please, you have the floor.

On behalf of the Women's Refugee Commission, we welcome this opportunity for dialogue. This year we mark the 75th anniversary of the Refugee Convention and the 65th anniversary of the UN Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness. Last year we marked 30 years since the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action. Yet in 2026, we're seeing millions of people impacted by rising displacement, restricted asylum space, statelessness, and discriminatory nationality laws, and a stagnation or regression on gender equality. A number of states are leading concerted efforts to attack and undermine international norms and UN conventions on women's rights and refugee rights. At the same time, statelessness rooted in discrimination remains woefully under-addressed. Your Excellency, how have you defended and advanced gender equality, refugee rights, and the right to nationality, and how would you rebuild political consensus and advance political action on these fronts? Thank you.

Thank you.
I thank the representative of the Women's Refugee Commission. Please.

I thank the representative for the question. The question on how to advance gender equality, I think that the Secretary-General must not only speak gender equality but must do gender equality. And I know that a lot of work has happened already in the senior-level management of the organization in terms of gender parity, and as Secretary-General, I would work to ensure that that also goes through the other layers of the organization to ensure that we have gender equality. But this is also an action for member states as well, and so working with member states, I think that we can continue to promote the issue of gender equality. Political action, I think the information that we provide to member states on what we are doing as the Secretariat would be important for countries to pursue political action. I believe sometimes the UN is the standard setter in certain respects and then it helps member states and in other cases we have good examples from member states that we could also use here. In the UN, but I recognize the various conventions that you mentioned and that there's still a far way to go in implementation.
Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Ecuador, followed by Equatorial Guinea and Liechtenstein.

Thank you, Madam President, and I'd like to thank Ambassador Caroline Rodriguez-Burkett for participating in these dialogues and presenting her vision of a possible mandate and also for the clarity of her responses which shows she knows a lot about all of these files. With regard to transnational organized crime, we're seeing this expand. It's one of the greatest and most complex challenges today for many countries. Its effects go beyond security and affect development, weaken democratic institutions, and can lead to levels of violence that are similar to active conflicts. And so, in the view of my delegation, this is a matter directly linked to the peace and security of our peoples. Ambassador Rodríguez, given your prevention focus and early warning and early responses of the UN, how would you promote greater focus of the UN to transnational organized crime issues and what mechanism would you promote to strengthen coordination between the various components of the UN system and regional organizations in the light of this phenomenon? And as a personal note, I appreciate, Carolyn, your standing, and I wish you every success in this challenge that you're facing, and I'm sure that with your abilities, which are fully recognized, you will be very successful. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Ecuador. Please, Your Excellency.

I thank Ambassador of Ecuador for his questions and for his kind words. On this issue of transnational organized crime, you're absolutely correct. This is part of the changing nature of the landscape which we operate in, and sometimes it appears as if those involved in transnational organized crime are ahead of those who are in enforcement, including in our member states. So collaboration and cooperation is extremely important. The work of the UNODC transparency is extremely important in this respect as well. And so the provision of information and sharing of information, I know that this is not— it could be a touchy subject in some areas, but as Secretary-General, it would be my role to also bring to the attention of member states the changing nature of what we see on the landscape out there, given the depth of information that the UN has from the various agencies. In terms of strengthening this component, I think that this is— in my time on the Security Council, I've seen, especially from colleagues in Africa, also speaking about this, and so the role of regional organizations where they exist would be extremely important. They're closer closer to the issues and sometimes are more equipped with the solutions that we may want to pursue. And so collaboration between the UN and various regional organizations, it's very important, and I would certainly promote that as Secretary-General.
I thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Equatorial Guinea, followed by Liechtenstein and Cuba.

Ambassador Rodrigues, allow me at the outset to congratulate you sincerely on being designated by the President of the Republic of Guyana as a candidate to the post of Secretary-General. I'd also like to express to you our great appreciation— in hearing your vision that was so clearly expounded. And I've got 3 questions, Ambassador. In UNAT, a lot of people are questioning whether the UN continues to be commensurate with the challenges upcoming. What would be the structural challenges that would define your mandate as Secretary-General in order to bring the UN together? And the second question is that the UN is facing a credibility crisis given the various complicated crises that are taking place at the moment. What would Your Excellency do any different to what is currently being done by the UN to ensure that UN80 is not just ceremonial, as it were, but a real inflection point? And then a third question. With geopolitical groupings ever more rigid, how would you ensure that UN80 doesn't create paralysis but, on the contrary, brings unity? Thank you.
Thank you. Please, Your Excellency.

Thank you for the questions, Ambassador. How to ensure UN aid is commensurate with the challenges that we face in addressing them? I think, like I mentioned before, the work that is ongoing, and I know that that work still has a far way to go in terms of the Workstream 3 on the structural and programmatic alignment, and that it is not yet clear in how that will move forward, but I know that there are discussions already ongoing on this. But this, I see, will be— will change the UN. It will be a change for the UN, but I believe that with the knowledge and the expertise peace of member states, that it would be for a better UN, a fitter UN, and perhaps a slimmer UN. We have many organizations, regional organizations that were not in existence when the UN was formed, and so recognizing the strengths of those organizations and how we partner with them would also be important as we move forward in this new UN. On the credibility crisis, I am not under any illusion of the geopolitical challenges that we face, but as I mentioned before, I think that the Secretary-General has to be proactive and to work with everyone to see where there are opportunities to move forward in bringing peace, of course, of development— I spoke a lot about that— But UN 80, I don't think it's going to be just ceremonial. I think we have to put in the work. Now, it's difficult work as member states, but as the Secretary-General, I think it's my role to give all the support to member states to provide all the objective information that they need so that we can make this UN better. It's very good, but we can make it better.
Thank you. Thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein, followed by Cuba and the Maldives.

Thank you, President, and thank you, Carolyn, for the conversation with us this morning. It's great to see you on the podium. I have two questions. The first is, I mean, we do believe that the power of the SG essentially rests in the ability to leverage the legitimacy that the Charter of the UN gives the position. But of course there is one article that gives a particular authority to the SG, and that is Article 99. So I'm interested in your thoughts on how you think the SG can best leverage Article 99 and whether you see formats— that are short of the formal invocation of Article 99, but also under what circumstances you, if chosen to be SG, would invoke Article 99, as Secretary-General Guterres has done one time during his tenure so far. My second question is, you've talked clearly about the duty of the SG to call out violations of the Charter, a statement we were very pleased to hear. How do you look at other violations, let's say violations of key bodies of international law such as the Genocide Convention, the law regulating crimes against humanity, and how do you see the division of work in this respect between the office you have put yourself forward for, and the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Liechtenstein. Please, Your Excellency.

I thank Ambassador for the questions. On Article 99, I think it would be important before invoking that article to have all the information of what is happening on the ground. Whether this is going to cause a severe humanitarian crisis in terms of what is happening on the ground, whether there have been severe violations, humanitarian and otherwise, on the ground. But also, I think it would be important for the new Secretary-General to speak to the parties. This would be extremely important before making a decision on invoking Article 99. So I know that this is an article that has not been used very much and that when it has been used, it's when it was a really challenging situation. But this is how I would approach it in terms of making sure I engage with the parties, making sure I know exactly what is happening on the ground in terms of violations and in terms of protection of civilians. Because if civilians are going to suffer immensely, I think it's important enough to bring that to the attention of the Security Council under Article 99. But let me say that in addition to Article 99, I think that there are means and ways of this for how the Secretary-General can— can be more in touch with the Security Council as well. We— having served on the Security Council just recently,— we have frequent consultations and I think in those consultations room, the Secretary-General can be present there as well. And so I will certainly make use of every avenue in that respect. On the issue of the Secretary-General and the Commissioner of Human Rights, I look forward to working very closely with all the heads of agencies, funds and programmes, and I think that I hope we will do a good job.

Thank you. We have 4 more speakers on the list, and perfect in time, so I would like to invite as the final speakers the distinguished representative of Cuba, the Maldives, Slovenia, and finally the observer of the League of the Arab States. Please, Cuba, do you have the Thank you, Madam President.

Dear Ambassador Carolyn, and personal congratulations on your designation. We are very happy to have these interactive dialogues as part of an effort to ensure that the selection process of the Secretary-General is open, transparent, and inclusive. We align ourselves with the statement delivered by the G77 and AOSA [FOREIGN LANGUAGE] and we'd like to put the following questions in our national capacity. What structural concrete reforms would you defend to transform the international financial system into something that's more just and representative that effectively responds to the needs and priorities of developing countries, including access to financing, debt alleviation, and a better voice and participation in decision-making? How do you see the role of the UN in that process? And the second question, given the growing escalation of conflicts and the proliferation of warlike rhetoric, what action would you take in the— as Secretary General to promote a culture of peace and the peaceful settlement of disputes and respect for the principle of non-use of force? I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. Please, Your Excellency, you have the floor.

I thank Ambassador of Cuba for the questions and to add to what I've said on reforms of the IFIs, I recall when my country was a heavily indebted country and some of us who were in that situation, some of our countries, we came together and we would advocate throughout the world for debt relief because in 1992 my country was paying 94 cents of every dollar in debt. There was no way you were going to come out of that without debt relief. And I recall when the UN started to speak up on this, that those who were concerned listened, and there was a change, and we were able to have debt relief. And so Guyana today is much better off than in that— during that time. And so I believe in the voice, the collective the voice of the UN. And so how we deal with the IFIs, I think the collective voice of the UN, plus the instruments that we are developing— we have the MVI, the Beyond GDP— this, I think, would also help us to, as we continue this engagement, to have the IFIs perhaps listen to us and we see it does not have to be major steps happening at one time, but it could be incremental.— all being geared to make sure that those who really need financing and who faces a very unfair situation now in terms of borrowing, for example, that this is changed. And as Secretary-General, I would continue to not just advocate on this, but to be at the forefront with Member States on this. On conflict resolution, all the tools that are available to me as Secretary-General, the good offices, I think that this is something we can use We can use more. My own country benefits from the good offices process of the UN, and as I said earlier, we do not put a cost to prevention, but these are some of the tools that, at the disposal of the Secretary-General, I intend to be proactive in putting at the disposal of member states. I thank you.
I thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Maldives, followed by Slovenia.

Thank you, Madam President and Ambassador Caroline. I have two questions. First, you emphasized continued support for climate commitments and also stressed that the resident coordination system has improved delivery at country level. How would you ensure that the Abbas is systematically reflected in the work of resident coordinators and UN country teams? Second, you also note a shift in the global risk landscape and the need for anticipatory decision-making, regional engagements, and timely UN action. As you would know, Sid's security concerns often arise less from conventional conflicts than from climate disruption, maritime vulnerability, food insecurity, transitional crime, and economic shocks. How would you ensure ensure that the broader understanding of security is reflected in the UN's work. Thank you.
Thank you. Please,

yes, first of all.

Thank you very much to Maldives for the questions. I spoke about the ABAS earlier, and certainly this is the blueprint for SIDS, and whatever we do as the UN and whatever we advocate for would be through the lens of the Abbas, and this includes the UN country teams, the Resident Coordinator System, of course. In terms of the global risk landscape and the— I get from what you're saying the connection or the link between climate and security. This is a discussion that I know is ongoing. During time again on the Security Council, members of the council were able to deal with this on a case-by-case basis in different situations. As you know, they deal with particular files, but I thought that that was a good movement by the Security Council in looking at the impacts of climate change and how that is a driver of conflict. And so those things would have to be built on, and as Secretary-General, of course, whatever is decided by the Security Council, by the General Assembly in this respect, we will certainly implement. But I think that we all are agreed that even though climate change may— for some, you don't see it as you would see it in a conflict, as I mentioned before, the effects— that it is causing serious challenges in different parts of of the world, where pastoralists, for example, have to move. Land is becoming scarce, and that creates a security challenge. So the impacts of climate change is widespread, and as your Secretary General, I would certainly be speaking on this. I know the current Secretary General, Mr. Antonio Guterres, has been a voice, a loud voice on this, and I intend to do the same.

Thank you.

I thank you. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Slovenia, followed as the final speaker for today, the observer of the League of the Arab States.

Thank you, Mr. President, and dear Caroline, congratulations and thank you very much for coming forward. All of us who have been working with you closely have really high respect for you. Respect for you as a diplomat, as a politician, as negotiator, consensus builder, but most of all, I think, as human being. And also today's discussion, I think, what came out very clearly, and I think we appreciate, is your passion— passion for the UN, your trust in the UN, and your commitment to the UN. And I think these are the qualities that we are looking for in the new Secretary-General, so thank you very much for giving us an option. I have to ask a question. You also are Administrator, and there hasn't been a lot of discussion today about financial situation. The budget of the UN depends— half of it comes— almost half of it comes from two member states, which probably, or is becoming more and more clear, that it's not sustainable. Especially if dues are not paid or are paid late. This is the issue for member states, of course, but you are affected as Secretary-General because you have to run the organization if you don't have money, and as I understand, around 50 countries are not paying. So I'm just wondering whether you had any reflections on how you're going to address, first, if the countries— when the countries are not paying,, or maybe to look for a different financial architecture for the financing of the UN? Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Slovenia. Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you to Ambassador of Slovenia. I've thought about this, Ambassador, and how to approach this as Secretary-General, because it's There are a number of complexities in this, but the bottom line is that we need to have the payments come in and to be engaged with member states, all member states, too, that are in the situation of having not paid and how we can work out a payment plan. But you're absolutely correct in terms of where the bulk of the money comes in, but as Secretary-General, I'm prepared to engage with everyone on this. I think that the formula that the UN has decided for payment, it's weighted equally for all of us, and so it's an obligation as well for member states to pay. And so this would be my approach in terms of engaging. There are also issues of when the money comes in, and sometimes you're not able to utilize it, and then it has to be returned., and so we have to deal with these issues, but this is going to be a really big focus because you can't do a whole lot without money. And so, yes, that's how I would approach that. Perhaps working out payment plans as well. I know some countries have had to do that, understanding the constraints. This is in addition to the larger countries, but the constraints that member states face. But thank you for raising that important issue.

Thank you. As mentioned, we have come to the end of this interactive dialogue, as we have no more speakers on the list. So as a final— as the final speaker, I will give the floor to the Observer of the League of the Arab States, also an opportunity to sum up for today. Please, you have the floor.

Thank you, Madam President, and thank you for convening this meeting, and thank you to Ambassador Caroline Rodriguez Beckett for presenting your candidature and for the brilliant presentation you made today. I will join the last speaker to say that, as always, focused, cool, confident, and action-oriented, and wishing you all the best of luck. The question that I want to pose is how would you SG benefit from and support the work done at the regional level on two counts. One count on the implementation of plans. We have Agenda 2063 for the African Union. We have the Arab Vision 2044-2045, and we have many other regional plans. And we have the Agenda 2030 in the UN, how best to combine the interests, the regional interests with the international interests in the implementation of those plans. The second part of it is related to how best to use the regional capacities in support of the United Nations in peace and security. What happened lately in the Gulf, what happened in Gaza, what happened, we see here a divide between the regional organizations and the United Nations, and sometimes between the United Nations and its member states working outside to try to settle the situations. How would you engage us in the regional organizations and help us help you? Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Observer of the League of Arab States. Please, Your Excellency, you have the floor.

Thank you, Ambassador, for the questions. As I mentioned before, when the UN was formed, we did not have the regional organizations and several other organizations, and we need to maximize our partnership as the UN with these organizations. The way I see Agenda 2063,, and also the Arab Vision 2044, they're connected to the Sustainable Development Agenda but go more into detail as to what these regions would like to see. And so I think the UN's work must be consistent with the agendas of the various regions and how we complement each other. We might be able to learn something that you are doing that might even be applicable elsewhere. —and similarly, I would say, from the UN, the support that we provide, given the vast experience that the UN has from other situations, I think could also be very, very helpful. And together we can build our combined capacities. Madam President, since this is the last time I would speak in the dialogue, let me just thank everyone for the questions. If you notice, I have approached the answers in very practical terms. I think that a lot of you know me here, so I did not have to go into detail of what I know and what I didn't know, but to approach the questions and to approach what's before us in a realistic way, in a practical way. And now that I have done that, I— what is just left for me to do is to ask you Thank you for your support to me for the next Secretary-General. Thank you.

With this, we have come to the end of this interactive dialogue. Before thanking you, Your Excellency, I would like to use the opportunity to thank the the many teams who worked hard in the last days to make the Interactive Dialogues of this week on short notice possible. Your individual contributions were seen and deeply appreciated by all member states. And I think this is also worth a round of applause to the whole team behind it. [APPLAUSE] And I would like to thank you, Ms. Rüdiger-Birkett, and all the participants, all the member states for your valuable contribution. The meeting is adjourned. I wish you all a good day. Thank you.
